$meta.note: One entry per stimulus. `description` is shown above the sketch. `prediction` is the stage-1 question (first zone), anchored on this scene's object and outcome. `outcome` is the same outcome as a noun clause, slotted into the two other stage-1 questions (what decides it, what you would change) and into the ranking prompt. `imposed` is NO LONGER READ by the app: the v2 protocol has no imposed counterfactual. It is kept because the model-side run still uses it, and check-study.mjs only warns on it. Description, prediction and outcome are given to the model verbatim. ALL NEED AUTHOR REVIEW before launch, against study/stimuli-contact-sheet.html.
$meta.rewrite: 2026-09-09: all 75 descriptions were rewritten as short human captions (mean 175 -> 83 characters, none longer than before). They are therefore NOT the descriptions used in the 2026-09-04 wave, so the stage-1 input differs between the two waves. That is accepted: the 04/09 data are ignored. All 75 still need author review.
descriptionRules: Write it the way a person would caption the sketch for someone who can see it: name the situation in a sentence or two, not the layout. Participants are not blind — 'on the left', 'in front of them', 'is in the air beside it' belong to the drawing, not to the caption.
Name the objects and how they are arranged. Never state or hint at what happens next.
Call the drawing convention 'the motion arrow', the same wording as the instructions screen.

Avoid the vocabulary of the concept list (friction, bouncy, stiff, pivot, balance point, heavier): describe objects in everyday words, so the description cannot supply the answer the list is meant to measure.

Same actor word on both sides. If the caption says 'a child', the question says 'the child', never 'the person'; if the question names a role (the sprinter, the parachutist), the caption names it too. A participant should never have to work out that two words mean the same character, least of all just before rating theories that a machine wrote about that character. `check-study.mjs` blocks on it, and warns when a generated theory or tool drifts from the scene's word.

The arrow convention is taught once on the instructions screen (and given verbatim to the model as drawingConvention). Do not restate it in every description; mention the arrow only when it is needed to say WHICH thing is moving.
questionRules: prediction: name the object and the outcome, never the property being varied. 'What happens next?' alone is ambiguous in timescale (people segment an event at several nested grains), so two participants answer different questions; naming the target collapses that variance (Battaglia et al. 2013 ask 'Will it fall?' and 'In which direction?', not an open question).

outcome: the same outcome as a noun clause, so block 2 can fix the outcome while leaving the change free. This is what keeps the participant's chosen attribute as the measurement (RQ2) while making answers comparable across participants.
Never two questions in one stem: lay respondents answer such items inconsistently (Adams et al. 2006, CLASS).
